questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is digestion?
options: The movement of food through the body
Breaking food into small soluble molecules the body can absorb
questions.answer: Breaking food into small soluble molecules the body can absorb
questions.hint: Think about why food has to be broken down — what does the body need to do with it next?
questions.explanation: Digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones so they can pass through the gut wall into the blood.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which enzyme breaks down proteins in the stomach?
questions.hint: Stomach acid plus enzyme — the name starts with P.
questions.explanation: Pepsin is the protein-digesting enzyme produced in the stomach. It works best in the acidic environment created by hydrochloric acid.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Amylase breaks down which food group?
questions.hint: The clue is in the name — 'amyl' relates to starch.
questions.explanation: Amylase breaks down starch into smaller sugars like maltose. It's made in the salivary glands and the pancreas.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Select all the enzymes involved in digestion.
questions.hint: Haemoglobin carries oxygen and insulin controls blood sugar — neither is a digestive enzyme.
questions.explanation: Pepsin (protein), amylase (starch), lipase (fats) and maltase (maltose to glucose) are all digestive enzymes. Haemoglobin is a blood protein and insulin is a hormone.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Put the parts of the digestive system in the order food passes through them.
questions.hint: Start at the top — where does food enter the body?
questions.explanation: Food goes mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (where most digestion and absorption happens) → large intestine (water absorbed) → rectum (faeces stored).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Where in the digestive system is most food absorbed into the blood?
questions.hint: It's long and folded with villi to give a huge surface area.
questions.explanation: The small intestine is lined with villi — finger-like projections that massively increase the surface area for absorbing soluble food molecules into the blood.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Villi in the small intestine are well adapted for absorption. Which feature is NOT a reason for this?
options: They have a thin wall (one cell thick)
They have a large surface area
They have a good blood supply
questions.hint: HCl is made somewhere else in the digestive system — think stomach.
questions.explanation: Villi are adapted for fast absorption: thin wall (short diffusion path), huge surface area, and rich blood supply (steep concentration gradient). HCl is made in the stomach, not the small intestine.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the main job of the large intestine?
questions.hint: By the time food reaches here, the nutrients have mostly been absorbed.
questions.explanation: The large intestine reabsorbs water from the watery mixture left over after the small intestine. What remains forms faeces, stored in the rectum.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. What does bile do to fats to help lipase break them down?
questions.hint: It breaks fats into tiny droplets — a one-word answer ending in '-ifies'.
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies fats, breaking large droplets into many tiny ones. This increases the surface area so lipase can digest the fats much faster.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
questions.hint: Bread, pasta, rice, potatoes — what do these have in common?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates (especially starch and sugars) are the body's main fuel. They're broken down to glucose, which respiration uses to release energy.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why does the body need protein?
options: For growth and repair of tissues
questions.answer: For growth and repair of tissues
questions.hint: Think about what muscles and skin are made of.
questions.explanation: Proteins are made of amino acids and are needed to build new cells and repair damaged tissues — muscle, skin, enzymes, antibodies.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: A lack of vitamin C in the diet causes which deficiency disease?
questions.hint: Historically affected sailors who couldn't eat fresh fruit.
questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency. Symptoms include bleeding gums and slow wound healing. Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits, peppers and leafy greens.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Iron deficiency leads to anaemia. Why does this make you feel tired?
options: Your blood can't carry as much oxygen
questions.answer: Your blood can't carry as much oxygen
questions.hint: Iron is in haemoglobin — what does haemoglobin do?
questions.explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells. Less haemoglobin means less oxygen reaches your cells for respiration, so you feel tired.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the name of the indigestible part of food that helps it move through the gut?
questions.hint: Found in wholemeal bread, fruit and veg — also called roughage.
questions.explanation: Fibre (or roughage) is plant material the body can't digest. It adds bulk to faeces and helps muscles push food along the gut by peristalsis.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of respiration?
options: To breathe air in and out
questions.hint: Respiration is NOT the same as breathing — it happens in cells.
questions.explanation: Respiration is a chemical reaction in every living cell that releases energy from glucose. Breathing (ventilation) just moves air in and out of the lungs.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Complete the word equation: glucose + oxygen → ___ + water (+ energy)
questions.hint: It's the gas you breathe out — two words.
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). The carbon dioxide is breathed out and the water leaves in breath, urine and sweat.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
options: Aerobic uses glucose, anaerobic uses fat
Aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not
Aerobic happens in plants, anaerobic in animals
Aerobic releases CO2, anaerobic releases O2
questions.answer: Aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not
questions.hint: The 'aer-' bit means air. So what's missing in anaerobic?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases lots of energy. Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen — it releases less energy and produces lactic acid in humans (or ethanol in yeast).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What waste product builds up in muscle cells during anaerobic respiration in humans?
questions.hint: Two words — it makes your muscles ache after sprinting.
questions.explanation: Without enough oxygen, glucose only partly breaks down and produces lactic acid. The build-up causes muscle fatigue and cramp during intense exercise.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: After hard exercise, why do you keep breathing heavily for a few minutes (oxygen debt)?
options: To bring in extra oxygen to break down lactic acid
questions.answer: To bring in extra oxygen to break down lactic acid
questions.hint: You owe your body something — what did anaerobic respiration leave behind?
questions.explanation: After exercise the body needs extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid that built up during anaerobic respiration. This 'paying back' the oxygen debt is why your breathing stays heavy.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Yeast carries out anaerobic respiration. The products are carbon dioxide and one other substance, used in brewing. Name it.
questions.hint: It's an alcohol — found in beer and wine.
questions.explanation: In yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. This process is fermentation. Brewers use it for the ethanol; bakers use it for the CO2 that makes bread rise.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
questions.hint: Tiny air sacs at the end of the smallest tubes.
questions.explanation: Alveoli are millions of tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. They give a huge surface area for diffusion.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which features make alveoli good for gas exchange?
questions.hint: You want a short diffusion path and a steep concentration gradient.
questions.explanation: Alveoli are adapted with huge surface area, very thin walls (short diffusion distance), rich blood supply (keeps the concentration gradient steep), and a moist lining for gases to dissolve.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: When you breathe IN, what happens to the diaphragm and ribs?
options: Diaphragm relaxes (domes up), ribs move down
Diaphragm contracts (flattens), ribs move up and out
questions.answer: Diaphragm contracts (flattens), ribs move up and out
questions.hint: Breathing in increases the volume of the chest — what has to happen to make more space?
questions.explanation: Inhaling: diaphragm contracts and flattens, intercostal muscles pull ribs up and out. Chest volume increases, pressure inside drops, air rushes in.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What process moves oxygen from the alveoli into the blood (and CO2 the other way)?
questions.hint: Particles moving from high to low concentration — one word.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration. Oxygen is more concentrated in the alveoli than the blood, so it diffuses in. CO2 does the opposite.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Smoking damages the alveoli, often causing emphysema. Why does this make breathing harder?
options: Alveoli walls break down, reducing surface area for gas exchange
questions.answer: Alveoli walls break down, reducing surface area for gas exchange
questions.hint: Emphysema destroys the structure that allows efficient diffusion.
questions.explanation: Emphysema breaks down alveoli walls, merging them into larger sacs. Less surface area means less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so sufferers get out of breath easily.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which substance in cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried in the blood?
questions.hint: It's a colourless, odourless gas — also produced by faulty boilers.
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen does, so red blood cells can't carry as much oxygen. That's why smokers get breathless more easily.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why does your heart rate increase during exercise?
options: To pump more blood, delivering more oxygen and glucose to muscles
questions.answer: To pump more blood, delivering more oxygen and glucose to muscles
questions.hint: Muscles are respiring faster — what do they need more of?
questions.explanation: Exercising muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration, and produce more CO2 to be removed. Heart rate and breathing rate both rise to keep up with demand.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: A student's resting heart rate is 72 bpm. During exercise it rises to 144 bpm. By what factor did it increase?
questions.hint: Divide 144 by 72.
questions.explanation: 144 ÷ 72 = 2. The heart rate doubled. Trained athletes have lower resting heart rates because their hearts pump more blood per beat (higher stroke volume).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why do well-trained athletes generally have lower resting heart rates than untrained people?
options: Their heart muscle is stronger and pumps more blood per beat
questions.answer: Their heart muscle is stronger and pumps more blood per beat
questions.hint: Think about what training does to the heart muscle itself.
questions.explanation: Training strengthens heart muscle so each beat pumps a larger volume (higher stroke volume). The heart doesn't need to beat as often at rest to deliver the same total blood flow.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Select all the functions of the human skeleton.
questions.hint: The skeleton holds you up, shields organs, lets you move and makes blood — it doesn't digest.
questions.explanation: Skeleton functions: support body shape, protect organs (skull, ribs), allow movement with muscles, and make red and white blood cells in bone marrow.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Muscles that work in pairs across a joint are called what?
questions.hint: One contracts while the other relaxes — they oppose each other.
questions.explanation: Antagonistic pairs work in opposition: when one contracts, the other relaxes. Classic example: biceps and triceps. Biceps contracts to bend the arm; triceps contracts to straighten it.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which pair of muscles works together at the elbow?
questions.hint: On the front and back of your upper arm.
questions.explanation: Biceps (front of upper arm) contracts to bend the elbow. Triceps (back of upper arm) contracts to straighten it. They are antagonistic.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What tough, flexible tissue attaches muscle to bone?
questions.hint: Not a ligament — that joins bone to bone.
questions.explanation: Tendons attach muscle to bone. Ligaments are similar but join bone to bone at joints. Cartilage cushions the ends of bones.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why is cartilage important at the ends of bones in a joint?
options: It cushions and reduces friction between bones
questions.answer: It cushions and reduces friction between bones
questions.hint: Think about what would happen if bare bone rubbed against bare bone.
questions.explanation: Cartilage is smooth and slightly flexible. At joints it cushions bones from impact and reduces friction so they slide easily. Synovial fluid also lubricates the joint.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: The elbow and knee are examples of which type of joint?
questions.hint: They only let you bend in one direction, like a door.
questions.explanation: Hinge joints (elbow, knee) allow movement in one plane — bending and straightening. Ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder) allow movement in many directions.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Order these from smallest to largest in size.
questions.hint: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs...
questions.explanation: Hierarchy of life: cells → tissues (groups of similar cells) → organs (different tissues working together) → organ systems → whole organism.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which is an example of an organ system?
questions.hint: Look for the answer with 'system' in the name — it's a group of organs.
questions.explanation: The digestive system is a group of organs (mouth, stomach, intestines, etc.) working together. The stomach is just one organ within that system.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
options: Breathing is moving air in/out; respiration is releasing energy in cells
Breathing happens in cells; respiration in lungs
Breathing is only in animals; respiration in plants
questions.answer: Breathing is moving air in/out; respiration is releasing energy in cells
questions.hint: One is mechanical (moving air); the other is chemical (in cells).
questions.explanation: People mix these up. Breathing (ventilation) is the physical movement of air. Respiration is the chemical reaction inside cells that releases energy from glucose. Breathing supplies the oxygen for respiration.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Air breathed IN is about 21% oxygen. Air breathed OUT is about 16% oxygen. What percentage of the inhaled oxygen was absorbed by the body?
questions.hint: Subtract the exhaled percentage from the inhaled percentage.
questions.explanation: 21% − 16% = 5%. Around 5% of the air's oxygen is absorbed each breath. The body doesn't take all of it — there's always more O2 inhaled than is used.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which is a long-term effect of drinking too much alcohol?
questions.hint: The liver is the organ that breaks alcohol down — so it bears the damage.
questions.explanation: The liver detoxifies alcohol but heavy long-term drinking scars it (cirrhosis), reducing its ability to function. Alcohol is also linked to addiction, heart disease and certain cancers.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the name of the addictive drug found in cigarettes?
questions.hint: Starts with N — it's why people get hooked.
questions.explanation: Nicotine is the addictive chemical in tobacco. It's also a stimulant — speeding up heart rate and raising blood pressure.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 1 Organisms
